question:
Which of the following statements about Airway Pressure Release Ventilation
(APRV) is FALSE?

options.text: APRV allows for unrestricted spontaneous breathing throughout the entire respiratory cycle.
It is a mode of ventilation that utilizes a prolonged time at a high pressure (Phigh) and a very brief time at a low pressure (P-low).

The brief release phase (T-low) is intentionally set short to cause gas trapping
and maintain end-expiratory lung volume.
To be effective and well-tolerated, APRV requires deep sedation and often neuromuscular blockade.
It is a lung-protective strategy that aims to recruit alveoli and improve oxygenation in ARDS.

correctAnswer: To be effective and well-tolerated, APRV requires deep sedation and often neuromuscular blockade.
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the False Statement:
Statement D is FALSE. A fundamental principle of APRV is the preservation of unrestricted spontaneous breathing throughout the respiratory cycle. Deep sedation
and neuromuscular blockade abolish spontaneous breathing, thereby negating the
specific physiological benefits of APRV (such as improved V/Q matching to dependent lung zones, preservation of diaphragm tone, and improved haemodynamics via
lower intrathoracic pressures during spontaneous inspiration). APRV is typically
used to reduce sedation requirements, not increase them.
Mechanism of Action:
APRV applies a high continuous positive airway pressure (P-high) for a prolonged
duration (T-high) to recruit alveoli and promote oxygenation. Unlike conventional
inverse-ratio ventilation, the exhalation valve remains open, allowing unrestricted
spontaneous breathing at any phase of the cycle. This spontaneous effort generates
negative pleural pressure, improving venous return and directing ventilation to dependent (well-perfused) lung zones, thereby improving V/Q matching compared to
passive positive pressure ventilation.
Controlled Gas Trapping:
The release phase (T-low) is brief (typically 0.4-0.8 seconds). It is insufficient for
complete exhalation, intentionally trapping gas to generate intrinsic PEEP (autoPEEP). This prevents alveolar collapse (derecruitment) during the release. The Plow is typically set to 0 cmH2O to maximise the expiratory flow gradient, but the
short time ensures the lung pressure never actually drops to zero.
Clinical Pearl
APRV Encourages Spontaneous Breathing:
Preserving spontaneous breathing improves ventilation of dependent lung zones
(improving V/Q match), enhances venous return during negative-pressure inspiration, and reduces sedation requirements.
CPAP with Releases:
This is a helpful way to conceptualize APRV. The patient is on a high level of CPAP
for most of the time.
Recruitment via Prolonged P-high:
The long duration spent at the high pressure level is what recruits and stabilizes
alveoli.

Ventilation via the Release:
CO₂ is cleared during the brief release phase from P-high to P-low.
T-low Determines Auto-PEEP:
T-low is set short (e.g., 0.4-0.8 sec) to terminate expiration early, trapping gas to
generate auto-PEEP. This prevents derecruitment during the release phase.
Setting T-low via PEFR Decay:
Set T-low to terminate expiration when the expiratory flow rate drops to 50-75% of
the Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR). This ensures adequate gas trapping to maintain end-expiratory lung volume.
Contraindications:
Avoid APRV in patients with severe obstructive lung disease (asthma/COPD) due to
the risk of excessive dynamic hyperinflation, and use caution in patients with raised
intracranial pressure.
Weaning Strategy ("Drop and Stretch"):
Weaning involves gradually reducing P-high (by 2-3 cmH2O) and extending T-high
(by 0.5-2.0 seconds). This transitions the patient towards CPAP as the releases become less frequent.
P-low Setting:
P-low is typically set to 0 cmH2O. This creates the maximum gradient for expiratory
flow during the brief release. The actual end-expiratory pressure is determined by
the timing (T-low), not the pressure setting.
Haemodynamic Benefits:
Spontaneous breathing during APRV lowers intrathoracic pressure compared to
controlled ventilation, potentially requiring less vasopressor support and improving
cardiac output via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
Monitoring Limitations:
End-tidal CO₂ monitoring may be inaccurate due to the variable flow and mixing of
gas during releases; arterial blood gas analysis remains the gold standard for assessing ventilation in APRV.
